title: Percentages, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with percentages, and then use Desmos to find an unknown original value and to solve a mixture problem.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. A sixty percent markup followed by a twenty-five percent discount is not a thirty-five percent increase. Students subtract the percents, but the changes use different bases.
Multiply the multipliers. One point six times zero point seven five is one point two, a twenty percent net increase.
Trap two. A price is sixty-eight dollars after a fifteen percent discount. Students add fifteen percent of sixty-eight, but the discount was taken from the original price.
To undo a multiplier of zero point eight five, divide by it. Sixty-eight divided by zero point eight five is eighty.
Trap three. From eighty dollars to one hundred dollars, students divide the change by the new value, one hundred, and get twenty percent.
beats.wrong_why: The new value is not the base

beats.say: The base is always the original value, eighty. Twenty divided by eighty is zero point two five, which is twenty-five percent.
Trap four. If eighteen of forty-eight students are in a club, thirty-seven point five percent are in it, and sixty-two point five percent are not. Reading carelessly gives the wrong group.
Read the question to see which group it asks for. Eighteen over forty-eight is thirty-seven point five percent in the club.
Trap five. Going from forty percent to fifty percent is a change of ten percentage points, but students call it a ten percent increase.
As a relative change, it is ten divided by forty, which is a twenty-five percent increase. The change in the percent itself is ten percentage points.
Multipliers are already the fast way, but Desmos helps when the unknown is buried. For the jacket problem, graph the sale price as a function of the cost, and a line at fifty-four.
We let x be the wholesale cost. After the markup and the discount, the sale price is one point six times zero point seven five times x.
Type y equals one point six times zero point seven five x. This is the sale price for any wholesale cost x.
Now type y equals fifty-four. This horizontal line is the actual sale price that the store charged for the jacket.
Click the crossing point. It is at forty-five comma fifty-four. So the wholesale cost is forty-five dollars, matching our answer.
Desmos also handles mixtures. How much water turns five hundred grams of a twenty percent salt solution into a sixteen percent solution? The salt stays at one hundred grams.
The salt is fixed at one hundred grams, while the total mass grows as we add x grams of water. So we graph the salt fraction as a curve.
Type y equals one hundred over five hundred plus x. This is the fraction of salt after adding x grams of water.
Now type y equals zero point one six, the target salt fraction.
Click the crossing point. It is at one hundred twenty-five comma zero point one six. So we need to add one hundred twenty-five grams of water.

Now a practice problem. A quantity goes up thirty percent, then down ten percent, and ends at two hundred thirty-four. What was the starting value? Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
Combine the two changes into one multiplier. An increase of thirty percent is one point three, and a decrease of ten percent is zero point nine.
One point three times zero point nine is one point one seven. So the quantity ends at one hundred seventeen percent of its start.
The final value of two hundred thirty-four is one point one seven times the starting value. Divide to undo it.
Two hundred thirty-four divided by one point one seven is two hundred. So the starting value was two hundred.
Check going forward. Two hundred times one point three is two hundred sixty. Then two hundred sixty times zero point nine is two hundred thirty-four, which matches.
To recap. Multiply multipliers, divide to undo, and always use the original value as the base for percent change.
beats.item: Multiply, divide to undo, original base

beats.say: Read which group the question wants, and tell percentage points apart from percent change.
Use Desmos for buried unknowns and mixtures. In the next topic, we study one-variable data.
